html:
Around 1500 BCE people sailed from island Southeast Asia, probably the Philippines, across more than 2,000 km of open ocean to settle the Mariana Islands in western Micronesia. It is one of the earliest long ocean crossings known anywhere, made before the Lapita voyagers moved out into the South Pacific.

The settlers were Austronesians. Their red slipped pottery, stamped with patterns, matches pottery of the same age in the northern Philippines. Their descendants are the Chamorro people of Guam and the other Marianas, and the Chamorro language is Austronesian.

Later Chamorro society built houses on latte stones, stone pillars topped with cap stones, from about 900 CE. The Marianas are also unusual in having rice before Europeans arrived, the only islands of remote Oceania that did. In 1521 Ferdinand Magellan stopped at Guam, the first European contact, and Spain later colonised the islands, which brought war and disease that cut the Chamorro population sharply.
